analysis.one_liner: Ends the antitrust exemption for health and malpractice insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has shielded the insurance industry from federal antitrust laws, letting health insurers share price data and coordinate in ways that would be illegal price-fixing in most other businesses. This bill would strip that protection from health insurance and medical malpractice insurers, making price fixing, bid rigging, and market division among them subject to the same antitrust rules as other companies. It was introduced by Rep. John Conyers in May 2012, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People and businesses buying health insurance and medical malpractice coverage, who would gain the ability to sue insurers for anticompetitive conduct and could benefit from federal antitrust enforcement against price fixing and market allocation among insurers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make health and medical malpractice insurers subject to the federal antitrust laws, ending their exemption under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, and would expressly bar them from price fixing, bid rigging, or market allocations in connection with providing coverage [S2] [S3].
It would also apply the Federal Trade Commission's ban on unfair methods of competition to the business of health insurance regardless of whether the insurer is organized for profit [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health and medical malpractice insurers, who would lose a legal shield they have held since 1945 and could face federal antitrust suits and FTC enforcement for coordinating on prices or dividing markets.

drawbacks.text: Insurers have long argued the McCarran-Ferguson exemption is needed for them to pool claims data to set rates in small or thinly served markets, where data-sharing antitrust rules could complicate rate-setting; the bill text does not address this industry concern [S3].

Removing the exemption would expose insurers to litigation and FTC enforcement costs, a burden that falls hardest on smaller insurers, and stronger antitrust enforcement does not by itself guarantee lower premiums where high premiums stem from market concentration rather than collusion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: a concentrated industry would lose a carve-out from competition law that no other major industry enjoys, and insurers engaging in price fixing or market division could be sued or prosecuted. The costs are real but modest and manageable — compliance and litigation burdens, mostly on smaller insurers — and they are costs the rest of the economy already bears. On balance the bill weighed clearly in favor of insurance purchasers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on May 18, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor [S4].

On June 5, 2012, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property, Competition and the Internet, where no further action was recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health and malpractice insurers kept their exemption from federal antitrust law, and their ability to coordinate on prices or divide markets remains shielded from challenge.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the antitrust exemption from health and medical malpractice insurers.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Lamar Smith (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the remainder of the Congress; referred it to a subcommittee on June 5, 2012, after which no action was taken.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and their trade associations benefiting from the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to repeal the McCarran-Ferguson exemption for health insurers during and after the 2009-2010 health care debate, when a similar measure passed the House; the exemption remained in place throughout the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of the chamber was never tested [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end the McCarran-Ferguson Act's exemption that lets health insurers engage in price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation without federal antitrust liability [S2] [S3]. Consumers paying premiums in concentrated insurance markets currently bear the cost of that exemption.

The bill would make malpractice insurers subject to the antitrust laws for the first time, removing a shield for coordinating on prices or dividing markets among doctors and hospitals who buy their coverage [S2] [S3].
